name: Idaho

notes: Food for home is taxed at the full rate. An income tax credit of $155 a person (up to $250 with receipts) offsets it, which isn't taken out here. Of the resort cities whose local option taxes are counted, Ketchum, McCall and Lava Hot Springs exempt groceries.

Alcohol is taxed at the sales tax rate, on top of excise taxes left out here: beer of 5% alcohol or less 15 cents a gallon; wine, cider and stronger beer 45 cents. Spirits are sold through the State Liquor Division's stores.

Cigarettes and other tobacco are taxed at the sales tax rate, on top of excise taxes left out here: 57 cents a pack of cigarettes and 40% of the wholesale price on other tobacco (no more than 50 cents a cigar).
Household supplies: diapers are taxed in full.
Personal care products: menstrual products are taxed in full; Idaho has no exemption for them.
Barber and beauty services aren't taxed.
Clothing is taxed in full; Idaho has no sales tax holiday.
Laundry and dry cleaning aren't taxed.
Motor fuel is exempt from the sales tax and pays 32 cents a gallon plus a 1-cent transfer fee instead, left out here.
Repair labor isn't taxed when it is listed separately from parts; parts are taxed.

Resort cities' local option taxes are counted where the city gives its rate (the local rates table names them); some also tax liquor by the drink: Sun Valley 4%, Ketchum 3%, Tetonia 3%, Driggs 2% and Hailey 2%, not counted here.

Hotel stays pay the 6% sales tax plus the 2% travel and convention tax, auditorium district taxes in some areas (5% in the Mountain Community Center District around McCall) and resort cities' lodging taxes; not counted here.
The services below are from the State Tax Commission's guides.
gaps: Idaho has no county sales taxes. Resort cities (10,000 people or fewer) may levy local option taxes, which the cities collect; the State Tax Commission lists 23. Counted where the city's own page or ordinance or the Secretary of State gives the rate: Stanley, Sun Valley, Ketchum, McCall, Victor, Driggs, Tetonia, Hailey (restaurants only), Donnelly, Cascade, Ponderay, Bonners Ferry, Lava Hot Springs, Riggins and Harrison. Noted on their pages, not counted: lodging-only taxes (Bellevue, Kellogg, Salmon, Sandpoint), Crouch's and Mackay's (reported only), and Irwin's and Swan Valley's (rates not confirmed; Swan Valley's voters adopted a 1% tax from January 1, 2027 on November 3, 2026, counted once it takes effect).

Lodging pays the 6% sales tax plus the 2% travel and convention tax, auditorium district taxes (Boise, Nampa, Idaho Falls, Pocatello-Chubbuck, and 5% in the Mountain Community Center District around McCall) and resort cities' lodging taxes; none is counted.

1606220: Bellevue's local option tax is 3% on lodging only (not counted); a November 2025 expansion to restaurants and liquor by the drink fell short of the 60% it needed (City of Bellevue).
1609370: Bonners Ferry's 1% local option tax (July 1, 2023 to December 31, 2033) exempts single purchases of $1,000 or more; it is counted in Bonners Ferry's rates on all taxable sales (City of Bonners Ferry).
1613150: Cascade's 1% local option tax, groceries and lodging included, is counted in Cascade's rates through 2026. Voters renewed it on November 3, 2026, 289 for and 157 against (65%; Idaho Code 50-1046 requires 60%; Valley County's unofficial count), from January 1, 2027 through December 31, 2031 as 1% on retail sales except groceries and single items of $1,000 or more and 3% on lodging in place of the 1% (Ordinance 744, ballot text). Groceries leave the tax on January 1, 2027.
1619720: Crouch levies 3% on lodging and 2% on liquor by the drink and prepared meals from January 1, 2022 for ten years (approved 43 to 22, as reported by KTVB); not counted here, since the city's own pages give only the 2021 proposal.
1622330: Donnelly's 1% local option tax is counted in Donnelly's rates; lodging also pays a 3% occupancy tax and the Mountain Community Center District's 5% (from June 1, 2026), which aren't counted (City of Donnelly, Ordinance 215).
1622690: Driggs' local option tax is 0.5% on retail sales and 1% on restaurant food; both are counted in Driggs' rates. Lodging pays 8% from January 1, 2026 and liquor by the drink 2%, which aren't counted (City of Driggs, Ordinance 494-25).
1634390: Hailey's local option tax is 1% on restaurant food, which is counted in Hailey's restaurant rate, plus 7% on lodging and 9% on rental cars (including a 2% added in November 2025) and 2% on liquor by the drink, through June 30, 2050; Hailey has no tax on other retail sales (City of Hailey).
1635200: Harrison's 1% local option tax on all taxable sales is counted in Harrison's rates (City of Harrison). Raising it to 2% on lodging, liquor by the drink, prepared meals and retail sales other than groceries, from January 1, 2027 through 2033, was on the November 3, 2026 ballot and failed: 65 for and 61 against is 52%, short of the 60% it needed (Idaho Code 50-1046; Kootenai County's unofficial count).
1640510: Irwin levies a local option tax (State Tax Commission list) whose rate wasn't confirmed; it isn't counted here.
1642580: Kellogg levies 3.5% on lodging (since October 1, 2015; not counted); the result of a vote on raising it wasn't found.
1643030: Ketchum's 2% local option tax on retail sales is counted in Ketchum's rates, with groceries and motor vehicles exempt; rooms and liquor by the drink pay 3% (City of Ketchum). Renewing the original tax from 2027 to 2041 and raising its retail part from 1% to 1.5% (lodging 2% to 4%) failed on November 3, 2026: 1,063 for and 944 against is 53%, short of the 60% a city local option tax needs (Idaho Code 50-1046; Blaine County's unofficial count). The original tax expires December 31, 2027 unless voters renew it, which the city says it could ask in November 2027 (City of Ketchum). The current rate is used here.
1645820: Lava Hot Springs' 2% local option tax is counted in its rates, with groceries, building materials, motor vehicles and auto parts exempt; lodging pays 5% (approved November 2024); a rise in the retail rate to 4% failed then (Secretary of State's canvass).
1648790: McCall's 1% local option tax for streets (January 1, 2026 to December 31, 2036) is counted in McCall's rates, with groceries and motor vehicles exempt; lodging pays 8% in local taxes plus the Mountain Community Center District's 5% (from June 1, 2026), which aren't counted (City of McCall; State Tax Commission).
1649240: Mackay levies a 3% local option tax on lodging, restaurant meals, liquor by the drink and equipment rental (as reported by the Post Register); not counted here, since no official source was found.
1664450: Ponderay's 1% local option tax (January 1, 2026 to December 31, 2035) applies only to purchases of taxable items totaling $999.99 or less; it is counted in Ponderay's rates on all taxable sales (City of Ponderay).
1667870: Riggins' local option tax is 1% on retail sales and 2% on prepared meals; both are counted in Riggins' rates. Lodging and liquor by the drink pay 2%, which aren't counted (City of Riggins, Ordinance 220). Voters renewed it for ten years on November 3, 2026, 127 for and 39 against (77%; Idaho Code 50-1046 requires 60%; Idaho County's unofficial count); the current rate is used here.
1671650: Salmon's local option tax is on lodging only: 4% since 2020 (approved in November 2019 for 15 years) plus 2% from January 1, 2026 (approved in November 2025), 6% in all; not counted here (City of Salmon).
1672100: Sandpoint levies 14% on lodging through 2035 (approved November 2022; not counted) and has had no retail local option tax since 2020. A 1% local option sales tax on all sales but lodging, from January 1, 2027 through 2036, was on the November 3, 2026 ballot and failed: 1,874 for and 1,721 against is 52%, short of the 60% it needed (Idaho Code 50-1046; Bonner County's unofficial count).
1676780: Stanley's 2.5% local option tax applies to everything subject to the state sales tax, lodging included (City of Stanley).
1678850: Sun Valley's local option tax is 3% on retail sales and 4% on restaurant food and drink; both are counted in Sun Valley's rates. It is also 4% on lodging, liquor by the drink, recreation memberships, rentals and admissions and 2% on building materials and ski lift tickets (City of Sun Valley). Whether groceries pay the 3% wasn't confirmed; they are counted at it.
1679120: Swan Valley is on the State Tax Commission's list of cities with a local option tax, whose current rate wasn't confirmed; it isn't counted here. On November 3, 2026 its voters adopted Ordinance No. 108, 122 for and 44 against (73.5%, above the 60% a city local option tax needs; Bonneville County's unofficial count): for seven years from January 1, 2027, 1% on sales subject to the state sales tax, 1% on liquor by the drink and 3% on lodging. It is counted from January 1, 2027, on the first build after it takes effect.
1680470: Tetonia's local option tax, from January 1, 2026 for ten years, is 0.5% on retail sales and 1% on restaurant food; both are counted in Tetonia's rates. Lodging pays 5% and liquor by the drink 3% (Ordinance 2025-05).
1684250: Victor's 1% local option tax on all applicable sales is counted in Victor's rates; lodging pays 8% (approved in 2025, to July 1, 2050), which isn't counted (City of Victor).

programs: Urban renewal areas (Idaho's tax increment financing, also called revenue allocation areas) are mapped statewide from the State Tax Commission's 2025–2026 taxing districts, each named with the city that holds most of it. Not mapped: business improvement districts (Boise's and Idaho Falls' downtown districts). Coeur d'Alene and Driggs are accredited Main Street America programs for 2026 (Idaho Commerce); Idaho has no enterprise zones.

warn.text: Coeur d'Alene draws many visitors (Lake Coeur d'Alene and its resort), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy over the city as a whole: its seasonal homes (4.4%) and its 45 lodging places (0.8 per 1,000 residents) fall under the flag's cutoffs, though 5 of its 13 census tracts are flagged on their own. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.

Boise draws many visitors (the state capital, Boise State football and the Greenbelt), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy over the city as a whole: its seasonal homes (1.1%) and its 101 lodging places (0.4 per 1,000 residents) fall under the flag's cutoffs, though 2 of its 65 census tracts are flagged on their own. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.
